title: Natural keys versus surrogate keys
description: A practical guide to explaining identifier stability when a source-system customer identifier changes, using a small hypothetical retail dataset and relational counterexamples.
lead: The hard part of natural keys versus surrogate keys is not naming the two categories. The hard part is explaining what should stay stable when a source system changes its mind. A source customer ID can be useful, unique today, and still be the wrong primary key for a long-lived analytical customer entity.

sections.heading: The stability question
paragraphs: A natural key is a key made from values that have business meaning. A surrogate key is an assigned identifier with no business meaning, usually created by the data model. The practical decision is not whether business meaning is good or bad. The decision is whether a value is stable for the thing the table claims to represent.

For practitioners, the most useful test is this: if the source value changes, did the real-world entity change, or did only one identifier for that entity change? If the person, account, product, or store is still the same entity, then the changing source value should not be the only identifier that other tables depend on.

This article assumes you already know what candidate keys and alternate keys are. The focus here is narrower: how to model a source identifier that changes without losing relational meaning. The example uses a hypothetical retail customer dataset. It is intentionally small so the counterexamples are visible.
bullets: Use a natural key as a primary key only when it is unique, required, and stable at the grain and time span of the table.
Use a surrogate key when relationships need an identifier that is independent of source-system value changes.
Keep important source identifiers as attributes, identifier-history rows, or scoped alternate keys instead of pretending they are irrelevant.

sections.heading: A hypothetical source identifier that changes
paragraphs: Suppose a retailer receives customer data from a CRM. The CRM emits a value called source_customer_id. In January, customer C100 is Ada. Ada places an order. In February, the CRM migrates Ada to a new identifier, C900. In March, the CRM reuses C100 for a different customer, Cara.

This is not a claim about how any particular CRM behaves. It is a hypothetical fixture designed to expose the modeling problem. The important point is that source_customer_id is unique in each daily extract, but it is not stable over the historical customer entity.
bullets: January: C100 identifies Ada.
February onward: C900 identifies the same Ada.
March onward: C100 identifies Cara, a different customer.
Orders arrive with the source_customer_id observed at order time.

codeExamples.code:
/* Illustrative relational fixture. Not a claim of execution. */

create table crm_customer_snapshot (
  snapshot_date date not null,
  source_customer_id varchar(20) not null,
  customer_name varchar(100) not null,
  migrated_from_source_customer_id varchar(20),
  primary key (snapshot_date, source_customer_id)
);

create table source_order (
  order_id varchar(20) primary key,
  order_date date not null,
  source_customer_id varchar(20) not null,
  order_amount numeric(10,2) not null
);

insert into crm_customer_snapshot values
  (date '2026-01-10', 'C100', 'Ada', null),
  (date '2026-01-10', 'C200', 'Ben', null),
  (date '2026-02-10', 'C900', 'Ada', 'C100'),
  (date '2026-03-10', 'C100', 'Cara', null),
  (date '2026-03-10', 'C900', 'Ada', 'C100');

insert into source_order values
  ('O-1', date '2026-01-15', 'C100', 40.00),
  ('O-2', date '2026-01-20', 'C200', 25.00),
  ('O-3', date '2026-02-15', 'C900', 70.00),
  ('O-4', date '2026-03-15', 'C100', 15.00);

sections.heading: Counterexample: making the changing source ID the primary key
paragraphs: A tempting design is to create a customer table where source_customer_id is the primary key, then point orders at it. That design looks clean when the first extract arrives. C100 identifies Ada, C200 identifies Ben, and orders can reference those values.

The trouble appears when Ada changes from C100 to C900. If the customer row is updated from C100 to C900, then the January order O-1 still contains C100 as the source value observed at order time. A foreign key from orders to customers is now broken unless the order is also updated or the foreign key is defined with an update action that cascades the changed key. Either way, the model has mixed two ideas: the identifier observed on the event and the current identifier for the customer entity.

The March reuse makes the failure easier to see. C100 now identifies Cara. If a model joins orders to the latest customer row on source_customer_id, O-1 can be incorrectly attributed to Cara. The join is syntactically simple but semantically wrong. The key did not identify one customer across the whole period being modeled.

This is the central distinction in natural keys versus surrogate keys: a natural-looking source value can be a valid key for one relation and an invalid key for another. source_customer_id may be a key for one daily CRM extract. It is not a stable key for the long-lived analytical customer entity in this example.
bullets: The January snapshot can use (snapshot_date, source_customer_id) to identify one row in that extract.
The long-lived customer entity cannot safely use source_customer_id alone, because C100 refers to Ada in January and Cara in March.
Updating facts to follow source ID changes can erase the source identifier that was observed when the event occurred.

codeExamples.code:
/* Counterexample: this join is unsafe for historical attribution. */
select
  o.order_id,
  o.order_date,
  o.source_customer_id,
  c.customer_name,
  o.order_amount
from source_order o
join crm_customer_snapshot c
  on o.source_customer_id = c.source_customer_id
where c.snapshot_date = date '2026-03-10';

/* In the hypothetical data, order O-1 has source_customer_id C100.
   On the March snapshot, C100 is Cara.
   A latest-snapshot join can therefore attribute Ada's January order to Cara. */

sections.heading: A better pattern: surrogate key plus identifier history
paragraphs: A more durable design separates the customer entity from the identifiers that source systems have used for that entity. The customer table gets a surrogate customer_key. A second table records source identifiers over time. Orders keep the source identifier observed on the event, and the modeled fact can also store the resolved customer_key.

This does not mean the natural identifier is thrown away. The source identifier remains important for lineage, reconciliation, and source-to-target diagnostics. It simply stops being the only thing that defines customer identity across time.

In the hypothetical fixture, Ada receives customer_key 101. Her CRM identifiers are C100 from January until the migration and C900 afterward. Cara receives customer_key 103. Cara also has CRM identifier C100, but only starting in March. The same source value can appear more than once in the identifier table when reuse over time is allowed, as long as the model can resolve an event date to one customer.

The SQL below is illustrative. It shows the relational shape, not a fully portable implementation of temporal uniqueness. A simple primary key, foreign key, unique constraint, and check constraint can express several table rules. Preventing overlapping validity windows for the same source identifier is a cross-row rule, so it needs a diagnostic query, a database-specific constraint, or a pipeline test.
bullets: customer_key identifies the modeled customer entity.
source_customer_id records what the CRM called that customer during a validity period.
Orders preserve observed_source_customer_id because that is part of the event as received.
Resolution uses the order date and the identifier validity window, not just the latest source value.

codeExamples.code:
/* Illustrative design for the hypothetical dataset. */

create table customer (
  customer_key integer primary key,
  customer_display_name varchar(100) not null
);

create table customer_source_identifier (
  customer_key integer not null references customer(customer_key),
  id_system varchar(30) not null,
  source_customer_id varchar(20) not null,
  valid_from date not null,
  valid_to date,
  primary key (customer_key, id_system, source_customer_id, valid_from),
  unique (id_system, source_customer_id, valid_from),
  check (valid_to is null or valid_to > valid_from)
);

create table modeled_order (
  order_id varchar(20) primary key,
  order_date date not null,
  customer_key integer not null references customer(customer_key),
  observed_source_customer_id varchar(20) not null,
  order_amount numeric(10,2) not null
);

insert into customer values
  (101, 'Ada'),
  (102, 'Ben'),
  (103, 'Cara');

insert into customer_source_identifier values
  (101, 'CRM', 'C100', date '2026-01-01', date '2026-02-01'),
  (101, 'CRM', 'C900', date '2026-02-01', null),
  (102, 'CRM', 'C200', date '2026-01-01', null),
  (103, 'CRM', 'C100', date '2026-03-01', null);

insert into modeled_order values
  ('O-1', date '2026-01-15', 101, 'C100', 40.00),
  ('O-2', date '2026-01-20', 102, 'C200', 25.00),
  ('O-3', date '2026-02-15', 101, 'C900', 70.00),
  ('O-4', date '2026-03-15', 103, 'C100', 15.00);

sections.heading: Worked result and diagnostic query
paragraphs: With the surrogate-key design, the expected customer totals are straightforward. Ada has O-1 for 40.00 and O-3 for 70.00, totaling 110.00. Ben has O-2 for 25.00. Cara has O-4 for 15.00. The fact that Ada and Cara both used C100 at different times does not collapse them into one customer.

The model also supports a useful diagnostic: detect overlapping validity windows for the same source identifier. Reuse over time may be allowed, depending on the business rules. Overlap is different. If C100 maps to Ada and Cara during the same date range in the same source system, an order on an overlapping date cannot be resolved deterministically without more information.

The following queries are illustrative SQL. They express the relational check and the intended resolution logic. Production implementations may use database-specific range types, exclusion constraints, temporal constraints, or pipeline tests.
bullets: Ada: 40.00 plus 70.00 equals 110.00.
C100 is not globally stable, but the combination of source system, source identifier, and validity period is usable for event-time resolution.

codeExamples.code:
/* Resolve source orders through identifier history. */
select
  o.order_id,
  o.order_date,
  h.customer_key,
  o.source_customer_id as observed_source_customer_id,
  o.order_amount
from source_order o
join customer_source_identifier h
  on h.id_system = 'CRM'
 and h.source_customer_id = o.source_customer_id
 and o.order_date >= h.valid_from
 and o.order_date < coalesce(h.valid_to, date '9999-12-31')
order by o.order_id;

/* Expected resolution for the hypothetical data:
   O-1  2026-01-15  101  C100  40.00
   O-2  2026-01-20  102  C200  25.00
   O-3  2026-02-15  101  C900  70.00
   O-4  2026-03-15  103  C100  15.00
*/

/* Customer totals after stable resolution. */
select
  c.customer_display_name,
  sum(o.order_amount) as total_order_amount
from modeled_order o
join customer c
  on o.customer_key = c.customer_key
group by c.customer_display_name
order by c.customer_display_name;

/* Expected result for the hypothetical data:
   Ada   110.00
   Ben    25.00
   Cara   15.00
*/

/* Diagnostic: find overlapping mappings for the same source identifier. */
select
  a.id_system,
  a.source_customer_id,
  a.customer_key as customer_key_a,
  b.customer_key as customer_key_b,
  a.valid_from as a_valid_from,
  a.valid_to as a_valid_to,
  b.valid_from as b_valid_from,
  b.valid_to as b_valid_to
from customer_source_identifier a
join customer_source_identifier b
  on a.id_system = b.id_system
 and a.source_customer_id = b.source_customer_id
 and a.customer_key < b.customer_key
 and a.valid_from < coalesce(b.valid_to, date '9999-12-31')
 and b.valid_from < coalesce(a.valid_to, date '9999-12-31');

/* Expected result for the hypothetical data: no rows.
   C100 maps to Ada until 2026-02-01 and to Cara starting 2026-03-01,
   so the validity windows do not overlap. */

sections.heading: Decision rules for practitioners
paragraphs: The clean explanation to stakeholders is this: a source identifier is evidence, not automatically identity. It may be the best available identifier in the source system, but the analytical model has to decide what entity remains the same when source values change.

When the source value is stable, mandatory, and unique for the full history you need, it can be a natural primary key. When it can change for the same entity, be reused for another entity, be merged, be split, or arrive late, it is usually safer as an identifier-history value. The modeled entity then needs its own stable key.

Dimensional modeling literature commonly distinguishes natural keys from surrogate keys and also discusses durable keys for tying together changed identifiers. Relational database documentation describes primary keys, unique constraints, foreign keys, check constraints, and exclusion constraints as mechanisms for enforcing table rules. Those mechanisms are valuable, but they do not choose the business semantics for you. The modeler still has to decide what the key means.

A useful naming convention is to reserve customer_key for the internal surrogate key and source_customer_id for the value supplied by the source. If the organization also assigns a durable business identity, name it separately, such as durable_customer_id. Avoid using a column name like customer_id when it is unclear whether the value is internal, source-provided, durable, or event-observed.
bullets: Ask: Can this value ever change while the entity stays the same?
Ask: Can this value ever be reused for a different entity?
Ask: Do facts need to preserve the identifier observed at event time?
Ask: Can two source systems issue the same value with different meanings?
If any answer is yes, separate entity identity from source identifier history.

takeaways: A source identifier can be unique in a snapshot and still be unstable for a long-lived analytical entity.
Surrogate keys are useful when relationships need to survive source identifier changes, reuse, merges, or migrations.
Do not discard natural identifiers; keep them as source identifier history, scoped alternate keys, or event-observed attributes.
The modeling question is not whether natural keys or surrogate keys are universally better. It is what value remains stable at the grain of the table.

title: Referential integrity across analytical tables
description: A practical guide to finding orphaned facts in analytical tables while allowing legitimate late-arriving dimensions to settle.
lead: Analytical tables often need referential integrity even when the warehouse does not enforce every relationship as a physical constraint. The hard part is not simply finding facts that do not join to a dimension right now. The hard part is separating true orphaned facts from facts that are merely waiting for a legitimate late-arriving dimension.

sections.heading: The practical problem
paragraphs: A fact table row is orphaned when it cannot be related to the dimension row it claims to reference under the model’s relationship rules. In a transactional database, a declared foreign key may prevent some invalid references from being written. In an analytical warehouse, the semantic requirement still exists even when a load process allows unresolved rows to land first: an order fact should resolve to the valid customer, product, store, account, or other dimension row required by the model.

The false positive to avoid is the legitimate late-arriving dimension. Kimball’s dimensional modeling material describes the case where facts from an operational process arrive before the associated dimension context. It also describes late-arriving facts, where the dimension keys must be found as of the time the delayed measurement event occurred. Those patterns mean the operational question should be narrower than “do all facts join to dimensions at this instant?” A better question is “which unresolved facts are still inside the allowed late-arrival window, and which are old enough to investigate?”

The diagnostic below uses a small hypothetical retail dataset. It assumes the reader already understands candidate keys and alternate keys. It does not depend on a specific warehouse engine, and the SQL is illustrative rather than executed here; adapt interval syntax, date literals, and common table expression syntax to the platform in use.

sections.heading: Model the relationship, not just the column
paragraphs: A common mistake is checking only whether fact.customer_key appears somewhere in dim_customer.customer_key. That is not always enough. In many analytical models, the valid relationship includes both an identifier and time. A fact from October 6 may need the customer dimension version that was valid on October 6, not merely any row for the same customer.

For this example, the dimension has a warehouse key and a source customer identifier. The source customer identifier is the business-side value used to match incoming facts before the final dimension key is known. The dimension is effective-dated, with one row valid for each source customer over a period of time. The fact table stores the order date, load date, source customer identifier, and, when resolved, the dimension key.

The audit rule is: an order fact is referentially valid when there is a customer dimension row with the same source_customer_id and the order date is within that dimension row’s effective period. If the stored customer_key is populated, it should equal that valid dimension row. If the dimension row is missing but the fact was loaded recently, classify it as pending rather than orphaned. If it is missing and older than the grace period, classify it as an orphan candidate.

This is a semantic check. It is not a performance prescription. In a large warehouse, the same logic may be implemented with persisted audit tables, incremental checks, partition filters, or data quality tooling. Those choices do not change the relational rule being tested.
bullets: Define the join predicate that represents a valid relationship, including effective dates when history matters.
Confirm that the dimension’s effective-date ranges are non-overlapping for the identifier being audited, or add a separate check for overlapping dimension versions.
Define a grace period based on the expected arrival pattern of the dimension feed and the risk of publishing unresolved facts.
Classify unresolved facts instead of immediately deleting, rejecting, or silently ignoring them.

sections.heading: A hypothetical retail fixture with counterexamples
paragraphs: The following illustrative fixture creates six order facts and four customer dimension rows. It includes a clean match, a legitimate pending late dimension, a likely orphan, a fact pointing at the wrong historical dimension version, a fact whose key exists but is not valid for the order date, and another clean historical match.

The audit date is 2026-10-12. The allowed late-dimension window is three days from fact load time. That means a fact loaded on or after 2026-10-09 can be unresolved without being called an orphan yet. This is a simple policy for the example; a real policy should be based on source-system delivery expectations and downstream risk.

codeExamples.code:
WITH
params AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-10-12' AS as_of_date,
         INTERVAL '3 days' AS late_dimension_grace
),
dim_customer AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM (VALUES
    (1, 'C001', DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '9999-12-31'),
    (2, 'C002', DATE '2026-10-05', DATE '9999-12-31'),
    (3, 'C004', DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-10-07'),
    (4, 'C004', DATE '2026-10-07', DATE '9999-12-31')
  ) AS d(customer_key, source_customer_id, effective_from, effective_to)
),
fact_order AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM (VALUES
    (1001, 'C001', 1,    DATE '2026-10-06', DATE '2026-10-06', 42.00),
    (1002, 'C003', NULL, DATE '2026-10-10', DATE '2026-10-11', 18.50),
    (1003, 'C005', NULL, DATE '2026-10-01', DATE '2026-10-02', 71.25),
    (1004, 'C004', 3,    DATE '2026-10-08', DATE '2026-10-08', 30.00),
    (1005, 'C002', 2,    DATE '2026-10-03', DATE '2026-10-04', 55.00),
    (1006, 'C004', 3,    DATE '2026-10-06', DATE '2026-10-06', 11.00)
  ) AS f(order_id, source_customer_id, customer_key, order_date, loaded_at, order_amount)
),
matched AS (
  SELECT
    f.order_id,
    f.source_customer_id,
    f.customer_key AS stored_customer_key,
    d.customer_key AS valid_customer_key,
    f.order_date,
    f.loaded_at,
    f.order_amount,
    p.as_of_date,
    p.late_dimension_grace
  FROM fact_order f
  CROSS JOIN params p
  LEFT JOIN dim_customer d
    ON d.source_customer_id = f.source_customer_id
   AND f.order_date >= d.effective_from
   AND f.order_date <  d.effective_to
)
SELECT
  order_id,
  source_customer_id,
  stored_customer_key,
  valid_customer_key,
  order_date,
  loaded_at,
  CASE
    WHEN valid_customer_key IS NOT NULL
     AND stored_customer_key = valid_customer_key
      THEN 'ok'
    WHEN valid_customer_key IS NOT NULL
     AND stored_customer_key IS NULL
      THEN 'dimension_exists_but_fact_key_unresolved'
    WHEN valid_customer_key IS NOT NULL
     AND stored_customer_key <> valid_customer_key
      THEN 'wrong_dimension_version'
    WHEN valid_customer_key IS NULL
     AND stored_customer_key IS NOT NULL
      THEN 'no_valid_dimension_for_fact_date'
    WHEN valid_customer_key IS NULL
     AND stored_customer_key IS NULL
     AND loaded_at >= as_of_date - late_dimension_grace
      THEN 'pending_late_dimension'
    WHEN valid_customer_key IS NULL
     AND stored_customer_key IS NULL
      THEN 'orphan_candidate'
    ELSE 'unclassified'
  END AS referential_status
FROM matched
ORDER BY order_id;

sections.heading: Read the results as decisions, not just failures
paragraphs: The expected classifications are straightforward when the relationship rule is explicit. Order 1001 is ok because customer C001 has a valid dimension row for 2026-10-06 and the stored key is 1. Order 1006 is also ok: customer C004 has a dimension version with key 3 that is valid before 2026-10-07, and the order date is 2026-10-06.

Order 1002 is not an orphan yet. It references source customer C003, no dimension row exists, and the stored customer key is not populated. However, it was loaded on 2026-10-11. With an audit date of 2026-10-12 and a three-day grace period, this row is still pending_late_dimension. The appropriate action is usually to keep the fact visible as unresolved, then recheck after the dimension feed has had time to arrive.

Order 1003 is the likely orphan. It references C005, has no resolved customer key, and was loaded on 2026-10-02. By the 2026-10-12 audit, it is ten days old, outside the three-day grace period. It should be routed to investigation, remediation, or a controlled unknown-member or placeholder policy if the dimensional model uses one. The important point is that the rule did not discard order 1002 while still finding order 1003.

Order 1004 shows why existence checks are weak. The stored customer_key 3 exists in the dimension table, but it is the C004 version valid before 2026-10-07. The order date is 2026-10-08, so the valid row is key 4. A check that only asks whether key 3 exists would pass a historically incorrect relationship. The better classification is wrong_dimension_version.

Order 1005 shows another counterexample. The stored customer_key 2 exists, and it belongs to C002, but that row is valid from 2026-10-05 onward. The order date is 2026-10-03. Under this model’s effective-date rule, there is no valid dimension for the fact date. This is not the same as a new dimension arriving late; the fact already carries a key, but the key does not satisfy the modeled relationship.

sections.heading: Turn the check into an operational contract
paragraphs: The diagnostic becomes useful when each status has an owner and an action. Treat ok rows as publishable. Treat pending_late_dimension rows as incomplete but expected; they should age out of that state or resolve when the dimension arrives. Treat orphan_candidate rows as defects that need triage. Treat wrong_dimension_version and no_valid_dimension_for_fact_date as modeling or processing defects, because a populated key can still be semantically wrong.

Avoid making the grace period a permanent hiding place. A row that is pending today should become either resolved or orphan_candidate after the allowed interval. That state transition is what prevents legitimate late dimensions from being discarded while also preventing old defects from accumulating invisibly.

Also avoid mixing unrelated questions into the referential check. The check should not decide whether the source identifier design is good, whether a surrogate key should have been used, or whether a nullable column has the correct semantics. Those are important design topics, but the audit here is narrower: given the model’s current identifiers and validity rules, can each fact be related to the dimension row it requires?

A practical implementation usually stores the results in an audit table with columns such as audit_date, table_name, relationship_name, referential_status, row_count, and sample_keys. Counts show whether the problem is isolated or systemic. Samples give operators a starting point without forcing them to scan the entire fact table. The example’s row-level query can be aggregated into those operational counts once the classifications are trusted.
bullets: Do not delete unresolved facts solely because the dimension is absent at first load.
Do not call a row valid merely because its stored dimension key exists somewhere in the dimension table.
Do age pending rows into orphan candidates when they exceed the agreed late-arrival window.
Do keep late-arriving fact handling separate from late-arriving dimension handling: delayed measurement events still need the dimension context that was effective when the event occurred.

sections.heading: A compact decision framework
paragraphs: Use this sequence when designing referential integrity checks across analytical tables. First, state the relationship predicate in business terms: for example, an order belongs to the customer row with the same source_customer_id that was effective on the order date. Second, identify the observation point: the audit date and the timestamp that starts the grace-period clock. Loaded_at is often more useful than event time for this purpose, because an old event can be newly ingested as a legitimate late-arriving fact. Third, define the grace period for unresolved dimensions. Fourth, classify rather than filter: ok, pending, orphan candidate, wrong version, or no valid dimension for the fact date.

The classification approach protects both sides of the problem. It protects data completeness by allowing legitimate late dimensions to arrive. It protects analytical correctness by refusing to treat stale unresolved facts, wrong historical keys, or invalid effective-date matches as acceptable. That is the core of referential integrity across analytical tables: not a physical constraint alone, but a testable relationship contract between facts and dimensions.

takeaways: Referential integrity in analytical models should test the full relationship predicate, including effective dates when dimensions are historized.
A missing dimension row is not automatically an orphan; use a defined late-arrival grace period to distinguish pending facts from orphan candidates.
A populated dimension key can still be wrong if it points to the wrong historical version or to a dimension row that is not valid for the fact date.

Late-arriving dimensions and late-arriving facts are related but distinct cases: one concerns missing dimension context at fact arrival, while the other concerns delayed facts that must be matched to the context effective at the event time.

title: Weak entities and identifying relationships
description: A practical guide to modeling records whose identity only makes sense inside a parent record, using a hypothetical retail order-line example and common counterexamples.
lead: Some records are not independently identifiable. An order line numbered 1 is not a real-world thing by itself; it is line 1 of order O-1007. Weak entities and identifying relationships give you a precise way to model that dependency instead of hiding it behind an accidental surrogate key or a vague child table.

sections.heading: The modeling problem: local identity is not global identity
paragraphs: A weak entity is an entity whose identity depends on another entity. It may have a local discriminator, sometimes called a partial key, but that discriminator is only unique within the parent. The parent’s key must be combined with the local discriminator to identify one child record.

An identifying relationship is the relationship that supplies the missing identity. In a relational design, this usually appears as a child table whose primary key includes the parent table’s primary key. The child’s foreign key to the parent is not just a reference; it is part of the child’s own identifier.

This is different from saying every child table is weak. A shipment may reference an order, but if the shipment has a carrier-assigned tracking number that uniquely identifies it, the shipment can be a strong entity. It depends on an order for business context, but not necessarily for identity. Weakness is about identification, not importance, ownership, or whether a row appears below another row in an application screen.

The practical question is: can a row be named unambiguously without the parent key? If the answer is no, the parent key belongs in the child’s candidate key. Normalization material frames related design choices in terms of dependencies: when a key is composite, non-key attributes should depend on the whole key rather than only part of it.
bullets: Use a weak entity when the child has a meaningful identity only within one parent.
Use an identifying relationship when the parent’s key is part of the child’s key, not merely a nullable reference.
Do not classify a table as weak just because it has a foreign key; many ordinary strong entities also reference other tables.

sections.heading: Worked example: hypothetical retail order lines
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical retail order system. The business creates order numbers such as O-1001 and O-1002. Inside each order, lines are numbered 1, 2, 3, and so on. Line number 1 can appear on every order, so line_number alone is not a candidate key. The pair order_id and line_number is the stable business identifier for an order line.
Here is a small fixture. The dataset is hypothetical and intentionally tiny so the dependency is visible.

Order O-1001 has line 1 for SKU A-RED with quantity 2 and line 2 for SKU B-BLUE with quantity 1. Order O-1002 also has line 1, this time for SKU C-GREEN with quantity 4. There is no conflict because O-1001 line 1 and O-1002 line 1 are different order lines.

The parent is order_header. The weak entity is order_line. The identifying relationship is order_header to order_line because order_id participates in the primary key of order_line. If someone says “line 1 shipped late,” the model should force the next question: line 1 of which order?
A relational implementation can express this directly. The following SQL is illustrative and PostgreSQL-flavored; it is included to show the constraints, not to claim execution results.

codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE order_header (
    order_id text PRIMARY KEY,
    customer_id text NOT NULL,
    order_date date NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE order_line (
    order_id text NOT NULL,
    line_number integer NOT NULL,
    sku text NOT NULL,
    quantity integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    unit_price numeric(10, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0),
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_number),
    FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES order_header (order_id)
);

INSERT INTO order_header (order_id, customer_id, order_date) VALUES
    ('O-1001', 'C-501', DATE '2026-10-01'),
    ('O-1002', 'C-502', DATE '2026-10-01');

INSERT INTO order_line (order_id, line_number, sku, quantity, unit_price) VALUES
    ('O-1001', 1, 'A-RED', 2, 12.00),
    ('O-1001', 2, 'B-BLUE', 1, 20.00),
    ('O-1002', 1, 'C-GREEN', 4, 5.50);

sections.heading: Why the composite key matters
paragraphs: The composite key states a business rule that a surrogate key alone does not state: within one order, a line number identifies at most one line. Across orders, the same line number may be reused. This is the core shape of a weak entity.

The primary key on order_line does two jobs. First, it prevents two rows from claiming to be the same line of the same order. Second, because order_id is also a foreign key, it requires every order line in the curated table to reference an existing order. PostgreSQL 18 documents the relevant mechanisms behind this pattern: primary keys, foreign keys, not-null constraints, unique constraints, and check constraints. Other relational systems expose similar concepts, though syntax and enforcement details vary.

The model also gives joins a clear semantic basis. If a revenue query aggregates order lines by order, the join from order_line to order_header is not optional decoration. It is the relationship that completes the child identity. That is why weak entities are often a better conceptual explanation than “a table with a composite key.” The composite key is the implementation; the weak entity is the meaning.

The expected totals from the sample data are straightforward. O-1001 has 2 times 12.00 plus 1 times 20.00, for an order total of 44.00. O-1002 has 4 times 5.50, for an order total of 22.00. The query below follows the identifying relationship from line to order and groups by the parent key.
bullets: The child key is not line_number; it is order_id plus line_number.
The foreign key is not merely descriptive; it contributes to the child row’s identity.
The design allows line_number 1 to appear many times overall, but only once per order.

codeExamples.code:
SELECT
    h.order_id,
    SUM(l.quantity * l.unit_price) AS order_total
FROM order_header AS h
JOIN order_line AS l
    ON l.order_id = h.order_id
GROUP BY h.order_id
ORDER BY h.order_id;

-- Expected result for the hypothetical fixture:
-- O-1001 | 44.00
-- O-1002 | 22.00

sections.heading: Counterexamples that look plausible but lose the rule
paragraphs: The most common counterexample is to add a generated order_line_id primary key and stop there. That design may be convenient for application references, but by itself it does not preserve the order-line identity rule. Without a unique constraint on order_id and line_number, the table can contain two different rows both labeled line 1 of order O-1001.

A surrogate key is not wrong. It becomes risky when it replaces the business identifier instead of supplementing it. If downstream systems need a single-column technical identifier, you can add one while still declaring the identifying candidate key. The important part is that the database and the data model both know that order_id and line_number must be unique together.

A second counterexample is to make line_number globally unique. That solves uniqueness by changing the business meaning. If the source system numbers lines starting at 1 inside each order, forcing global line numbers invents a new identifier that users cannot reconcile with the operational record. You may still create a technical sequence, but it should not masquerade as the natural order-line identity.

A third counterexample is to model SKU as part of the order-line key. That fails when the same SKU appears twice on one order for legitimate reasons, such as separate fulfillment rules, promotional pricing, or manual entry behavior. SKU is an attribute of the line in this example, not the line’s identifier. If the business actually says one SKU can appear only once per order, that is a separate uniqueness rule on order_id and sku, not a replacement for the line identity unless the business also identifies lines that way.
The following table definition is a useful anti-pattern. It has a primary key, and it has a foreign key, but it does not enforce the identifying relationship’s local uniqueness rule.

codeExamples.code:
CREATE TABLE order_line_bad (
    order_line_id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES order_header (order_id),
    line_number integer NOT NULL,
    sku text NOT NULL,
    quantity integer NOT NULL
);

-- These two rows should not both be allowed if line_number identifies a line within an order.
INSERT INTO order_line_bad (order_line_id, order_id, line_number, sku, quantity) VALUES
    (10, 'O-1001', 1, 'A-RED', 2),
    (11, 'O-1001', 1, 'D-YELLOW', 1);

-- If a surrogate key is needed, keep the identifying rule as a unique constraint.
CREATE TABLE order_line_with_surrogate (
    order_line_id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    order_id text NOT NULL REFERENCES order_header (order_id),
    line_number integer NOT NULL,
    sku text NOT NULL,
    quantity integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
    UNIQUE (order_id, line_number)
);

sections.heading: Diagnostic for existing tables
paragraphs: When reviewing an existing model, do not start by asking whether a table has a composite primary key. Start by asking how users, source systems, or contracts identify one record. A table can have a surrogate primary key and still represent a weak entity if its real-world identifier depends on a parent.

Use this diagnostic sequence. First, name the parent entity. Second, name the child record using business language. Third, try to identify the child without the parent. Fourth, test whether the apparent child identifier repeats across parents. Fifth, check whether the database enforces the parent-plus-local-identifier rule.

For a staging table, the checks below can reveal whether the data behaves like a weak entity before constraints are added to a curated table. The queries are illustrative; adapt column names, null handling, and source-system rules before using the pattern in a real pipeline.

The duplicate check should return no rows after curation if order_id and line_number define the order-line identity. In raw ingestion it may return rows because of file replays, late corrections, or source defects. That does not change the conceptual model; it tells you the pipeline needs deduplication or exception handling before loading the constrained table.

The orphan check should also return no rows in the curated model. If an order line arrives before its order header, that is an ingestion timing problem. The relational model should still represent the rule that a line belongs to an order. You may stage the child temporarily, but the final table should not silently accept an order line whose parent never exists.
bullets: Can the child be identified without naming the parent? If not, suspect a weak entity.
Does the same local identifier repeat under different parents? If yes, the local identifier is not globally unique.
Does the database enforce the parent-plus-local-identifier candidate key? If not, the model may depend on undocumented application behavior.
Would deleting or correcting the parent change the validity of the child? If yes, define the referential action intentionally rather than leaving it accidental.

codeExamples.code:
-- Duplicate local identifiers within the same parent.
SELECT
    order_id,
    line_number,
    COUNT(*) AS row_count
FROM raw_order_line
GROUP BY order_id, line_number
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

-- Local identifiers that repeat across parents. This is expected for a weak entity.
SELECT
    line_number,
    COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS parent_count
FROM raw_order_line
GROUP BY line_number
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) > 1;

-- Child rows without a parent in the curated relationship.
SELECT l.*
FROM raw_order_line AS l
LEFT JOIN order_header AS h
    ON h.order_id = l.order_id
WHERE h.order_id IS NULL;

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and boundaries
paragraphs: Composite keys make the identifying relationship explicit, but they also propagate more columns into referencing tables. That can be awkward in wide schemas, event payloads, or tools that assume single-column identifiers. The usual compromise is to keep the composite candidate key and add a surrogate technical key when needed. The surrogate supports convenience; the composite unique constraint preserves meaning.

Referential actions also require a policy decision. If an order is deleted, should its lines be deleted automatically, deletion blocked, or the order retained with a status change instead of physical deletion? Identifying relationships often suggest existence dependency, but they do not by themselves choose a deletion policy. In many analytical systems, immutable facts and audit requirements lead teams to avoid physical deletion and instead model cancellation, reversal, or invalidation states.

Weak entities are also not the same thing as hierarchies. A store department, category, and subcategory hierarchy may have parent-child relationships, but each node might still have its own durable identifier. Kimball’s dimensional modeling material discusses ragged or variable-depth hierarchies as uneven tree structures that can be represented with bridge tables or path strings for analysis. That is a hierarchy modeling problem, not automatically a weak-entity identity problem. The test remains the same: does the child’s identifier require the parent’s key?

Finally, keep this topic separate from general relationship multiplicity. A weak entity commonly has one owner and many sibling records under that owner, but the identifying question is narrower: what columns are required to identify one child record correctly?

sections.heading: A practical rule for practitioners
paragraphs: Model a record as a weak entity when its natural name is incomplete without its parent. In the retail example, “order line 1” is incomplete; “order O-1001, line 1” is complete. That wording maps directly to the relational key: order_id plus line_number.

Then decide whether you also need a surrogate key. If you do, add it without deleting the identifying constraint. This avoids the false choice between operational convenience and relational correctness. A single-column technical key can coexist with the composite candidate key that expresses the business rule.

The best outcome is a model where invalid data is hard to insert and valid data is easy to explain. Weak entities and identifying relationships are useful because they turn a common ambiguity into a concrete design: the parent key is part of the child’s identity.

takeaways: A weak entity is identified by combining a parent key with a local discriminator; the local discriminator is not globally unique on its own.
An identifying relationship is usually implemented by including the parent key in the child table’s primary key or in a declared candidate key enforced by a unique constraint.
Surrogate keys can be useful, but they should not replace the parent-plus-local-identifier rule when that rule defines the real-world identity.
Use diagnostics on existing tables to find duplicate child identifiers within a parent, expected reuse across parents, and child rows with no valid parent.
